qs.q: A 35-year-old patient presents with fatigue, weight loss, and hyperpigmentation of the palmar creases. Laboratory tests reveal hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia. What is the primary mechanism responsible for the hyperkalaemia?
o: Aldosterone deficiency leading to impaired renal potassium excretion
Excess cortisol causing a shift of potassium out of cells
Pituitary failure resulting in direct suppression of distal tubules
Increased renin activity driving excessive reabsorption of potassium
qs.e: Aldosterone promotes potassium excretion in the collecting duct, so its deficiency in primary adrenal insufficiency causes potassium retention. Cortisol deficiency impairs gluconeogenesis but does not directly cause hyperkalaemia.

qs.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with fatigue, weight loss, and hyperpigmentation of the skin. Laboratory tests reveal hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia. Which underlying mechanism best explains her physical findings?
o: Deficient aldosterone production without high ACTH
Increased renin activity secondary to renal ischemia
qs.e: Primary adrenal insufficiency leads to an elevated ACTH level, which stimulates melanocytes and causes hyperpigmentation, along with electrolyte imbalances. Secondary insufficiency does not cause hyperpigmentation because aldosterone remains intact and ACTH is suppressed or low.

qs.q: A patient is evaluated for a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Laboratory results show hyperkalaemia, a urine pH greater than 5.5, and a mildly low serum bicarbonate level. Which type of renal tubular acidosis is most consistent with these findings?
qs.e: Type 4 Renal Tubular Acidosis is uniquely identified by hyperkalaemia, distinguishing it from Types 1 and 2 which present with hypokalaemia. Types 1 and 2 typically present with low serum potassium levels.
qs.s: Adrenal Adenoma vs Carcinoma: Diagnostic Criteria — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with long-standing poorly controlled diabetes mellitus develops a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Serum electrolytes reveal hyperkalaemia. Which type of renal tubular acidosis is most consistent with this presentation?
qs.e: Type 4 RTA is the only form of renal tubular acidosis characterized by hyperkalaemia due to hypoaldosteronism, and it is frequently caused by diabetic nephropathy. Types 1 and 2 RTA characteristically present with hypokalaemia.
qs.s: Adrenal Adenoma vs Carcinoma: Illustrated Review — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: A neonate presents with a salt-wasting crisis, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, and early signs of virilisation. Laboratory workup confirms congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Which enzymatic deficiency is the most common cause of this presentation?
qs.e: 21-hydroxylase deficiency is by far the most common cause of congenital adrenal hyperplasia, resulting in decreased cortisol and aldosterone synthesis alongside an overproduction of androgens. This block leads to salt-wasting and virilisation.

qs.q: Which drug class is a recognized cause of hyperkalaemia by reducing distal tubular potassium secretion?
o: Loop active diuretics such as furosemide
qs.e: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics, beta-blockers, and NSAIDs can cause hyperkalaemia by reducing distal tubular potassium secretion. Loop diuretics typically promote renal potassium loss instead.

qs.q: What is the primary purpose of administering calcium gluconate in the management of severe hyperkalaemia?
o: To protect the cardiac muscle from toxicity
To shift potassium rapidly into intracellular fluid
To exchange sodium for potassium in the gut lumen
To promote renal excretion of excess potassium
qs.e: Calcium gluconate is used to protect cardiac muscle from the toxic effects of hyperkalaemia. Intracellular shifts are achieved using insulin, dextrose, bicarbonate, or beta-agonists.

qs.q: In a patient with chronic interstitial nephritis, which clinical feature is typically more severe compared to other forms of renal disease, often resulting in hyperkalaemia and acidosis?
o: Electrolyte abnormalities due to tubular unresponsiveness
Hematuria with dysmorphic red blood cells
qs.e: Chronic interstitial nephritis is characterized by tubular damage leading to significant electrolyte disturbances such as hyperkalaemia and acidosis. Proteinuria in this condition is typically modest, usually less than 1g/day.

rx.name: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes
first: Calcium gluconate IV to protect the heart
Insulin with dextrose and nebulised salbutamol to shift potassium into cells

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Hyperkalaemia is an elevated serum potassium level that can cause life‑threatening cardiac arrhythmias. Diagnosis relies on lab values and ECG changes, and treatment must act quickly to protect the heart and lower potassium.

sections.p: Hyperkalaemia is defined as serum potassium >5.0 mmol/L. Diagnosis requires a reliable potassium measurement and assessment for ECG abnormalities.
b: Serum K+ >5.0 mmol/L confirms the diagnosis
ECG changes guide urgency of treatment

sections.p: Severity guides management urgency and choice of interventions.
b: Mild: 5.1‑5.9 mmol/L, usually no ECG changes
Moderate: 6.0‑6.4 mmol/L, may show peaked T waves
Severe: ≥6.5 mmol/L or any ECG abnormality, high risk of arrhythmia

sections.p: Identify the underlying driver to stop further potassium rise.
b: Renal failure (acute or chronic) – most common
Potassium‑sparing drugs (spironolactone, ACE‑I, ARB, NSAIDs)
Cellular shift (acidosis, insulin deficiency, β‑blocker overdose)
Massive tissue breakdown (rhabdomyolysis, hemolysis, burns)
Tropical infections causing renal injury (malaria, severe dengue, schistosomiasis)
Herbal remedies high in potassium

sections.p: Symptoms are often nonspecific; cardiac signs dominate.
b: Muscle weakness or paresthesia
Palpitations, chest discomfort
Nausea, vomiting
ECG: peaked T waves → widened QRS → sine‑wave pattern

sections.p: Tests must answer why potassium is high and whether the heart is affected.

t.b: What is the exact potassium level? Guides severity staging
Are there arrhythmic changes? Determines need for immediate calcium
Is the kidney unable to excrete potassium? Directs removal strategy
Is there metabolic acidosis causing a shift? Helps decide shift therapy
Which drugs could be raising potassium? Guides cessation

sections.p: Rapidly rising potassium can cause fatal arrhythmias.
b: ECG changes (peaked T, widened QRS, sine wave)
Sudden cardiac arrest
Severe metabolic acidosis

sections.p: Treat the heart first, then shift potassium intracellularly, and finally remove excess.
b: IV calcium gluconate if ECG changes – stabilises myocardial membrane
Insulin + dextrose (or IV glucose) – drives K+ into cells
Nebulised salbutamol – β2 agonist shift without glucose load
Loop diuretic (if urine output) – promotes renal excretion
Sodium bicarbonate if severe acidosis – shifts K+ and corrects pH
Dialysis for refractory or renal failure cases – definitive removal

sections.p: Prevent recurrence by addressing chronic causes and monitoring.
b: Regular potassium checks in CKD or on potassium‑sparing drugs
Educate patients on low‑potassium diet and avoiding herbal supplements
Adjust or stop offending medications

sections.p: Conditions that mimic ECG or symptom patterns.
b: Hypokalaemia – can also cause arrhythmias but shows flattened T waves
Hypercalcaemia – may cause shortened QT, not peaked T
Hemolysed blood sample falsely raises potassium – repeat if suspicion
Delayed ECG after treatment may still show changes despite safe potassium

whenToSeekHelp: New or worsening chest pain, syncope, or palpitations with any ECG abnormality
Severe muscle weakness progressing to paralysis
Rapid rise in potassium (>6.5 mmol/L) on repeat testing

faq.a: Calcium stabilises cardiac membranes immediately, while insulin works slower to shift potassium.

faq.q: Can oral potassium binders be used in emergencies?
faq.a: They act over hours and are not suitable for acute life‑threatening hyperkalaemia.
Maximise diuretics, give repeated insulin/dextrose, and consider sodium polystyrene sulfonate if safe.
